propositions.text: This is a judicial review under s. 22(1) of the Citizenship Act of a Citizenship Judge's decision approving Respondent's citizenship application.
Applicant challenges the Citizenship Judge's decision, alleging error in finding Respondent established residence after initial six-day stay.

paragraphs.summary: Court states this is a judicial review of a Citizenship Judge's approval of Respondent's citizenship; Applicant alleges error in residence finding.

propositions.text: After considering the record and submissions, the application must be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes application must be dismissed after considering record and submissions.

propositions.text: Respondent is a UK citizen, landed permanent resident in Canada on January 2, 2008 at age 17.
Respondent left Canada six days later to complete final high school semester in France; family remained in Victoria, BC.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Respondent is UK citizen landed in Canada in 2008 at 17, left after six days to study in France; family stayed in Victoria.

propositions.text: Respondent completed dual law degree in London and Paris from Sept 2008 to June 2012, then Legal Practice Course in London 2012-2013.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Respondent completed dual law degree in London and Paris and Legal Practice Course in London.

propositions.text: Respondent returned to Canada for short visits; total physical presence from March 10, 2008 to March 10, 2012 unclear but differences insignificant.
Respondent's application listed 10 absences totaling 1178 days; questionnaire listed 11 absences totaling 1202 days; officer revised to 1183 days absence, 277 days presence, shortfall of 818 days.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Respondent's physical presence in Canada during relevant period is unclear but shortfall of 818 days from required 1095 days.

propositions.text: Respondent visited Canada summers 2008-2011, worked at Tim Hortons, dress shop, and father's painting business during visits.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Respondent worked various jobs in Canada during summer visits from 2008 to 2011.

propositions.text: Respondent completed Canadian citizenship application on March 10, 2012 while residing in UK.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Respondent applied for Canadian citizenship in March 2012 while in UK.

propositions.text: Respondent returned to Canada in May 2012 and volunteered at a law firm in Victoria for four weeks in June and July 2012.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Respondent volunteered at a Victoria law firm during summer 2012 visit.

propositions.text: Record unclear when Respondent returned to Canada or duration after 2013 Legal Practice course, but attended citizenship judge interviews in July 2013 and October 2014.

paragraphs.summary: Court states record unclear on Respondent's post-2013 Canada presence but she attended citizenship judge interviews in 2013 and 2014.

propositions.text: Citizenship judge approved Respondent's application applying Re Papadogiorgakis residency test.
Respondent centralized mode of living as minor child with family in Victoria, BC despite less than a week initial stay.
Absences were temporary for studies and did not break continuity of ordinary mode of living with family in Canada.
Respondent returned frequently at Christmas and summer holidays.
Engaged in Canadian society during visits through employment and social/charitable activity.
Left bulk of belongings at parents' home and was totally dependent on parents during period.
Completed studies in June 2013 with law degrees from UK and France.
In July 2013, Respondent informed citizenship judge of intention to remain in Canada and get accredited as lawyer.
Respondent must be Canadian citizen to practice law in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker found Respondent centralized living in Canada as minor, absences temporary, engaged socially and employed, dependent on parents, intended to remain and practice law.

propositions.text: Issue is whether Citizenship judge erred interpreting residence requirement, especially initial residency established before six-day departure.

paragraphs.summary: Court states issue is whether Citizenship judge erred in interpreting residence requirement and initial residency finding.

propositions.text: Subsection 5(1)(c) Citizenship Act requires lawful admission, retention of permanent resident status, and at least three years residence in Canada within four years before application.

paragraphs.summary: Court states s.5(1)(c) requires lawful admission, retention of status, and three years residence in Canada within four years.

propositions.text: Residence criterion is issue; not defined in Act; three tests have emerged in jurisprudence to determine residency.
Court recently summarized these tests in Boland v Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, 2015 FC 376.

paragraphs.summary: Court states residence is issue, not defined in Act, with three jurisprudential tests summarized in Boland.

propositions.text: Re Papadogiorgakis test assesses quality of attachment to Canada; absences count if temporary and intention to establish permanent home shown.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Re Papadogiorgakis test assesses attachment and temporary absences with intention to establish permanent home.

propositions.text: Re Pourghasemi test requires physical presence in Canada for at least 1095 days during relevant period to satisfy residency.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Re Pourghasemi test requires physical presence of at least 1095 days to satisfy residency.

propositions.text: Re Koo test combines elements, requiring applicant to regularly/customarily live or centralize mode of existence in Canada, guided by six factors.

paragraphs.summary: Court states Re Koo test requires applicant to regularly live or centralize existence in Canada, guided by six factors.

propositions.text: Applicant does not dispute Citizenship judge could apply any of the three tests or choice of centralized mode of living test.
Applicant argues Citizenship judge misapplied chosen test and failed to properly assess evidence.
Issue is mixed fact and law; citizenship judges owed deference due to expertise; review standard is reasonableness.
Chief Justice in Huang v Canada supports reasonableness standard for citizenship judge decisions.
Supreme Court decisions confirm review of citizenship judge matters on reasonableness standard.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues misapplication of test; court states issue is mixed fact and law with deference and reasonableness standard supported by case law.

propositions.text: Applicant argues Citizenship judge erred finding Respondent established residency after six days and failed to provide reasons.
Applicant argues Citizenship judge misapplied Papadogiorgakis test and erred in finding residence based on commitment, dependency, and intention.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Citizenship judge erred in initial residency finding and misapplied Papadogiorgakis test based on commitment and dependency.

propositions.text: To meet residence requirements, applicant must show by objective facts initial residence established in Canada.
Ahmed v Canada and other cases distinguish issue of establishing residence from maintaining residence.

paragraphs.summary: Court states applicant must show initial residence by objective facts; Ahmed and others distinguish establishing from maintaining residence.

propositions.text: Court disagrees with Applicant that Citizenship judge gave no reasons for initial residence finding; reasons could be more explicit but are present.

Citizenship judge found Respondent centralized mode of living despite six-day departure for reasons including minor status, temporary absences, belongings left in Canada, frequent returns, employment, volunteering, family events, driver's license, and law accreditation efforts.
Citizenship judge erred in holding Respondent needed citizenship to practice law in Canada, per Andrews v Law Society of BC.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Citizenship judge gave reasons for initial residence finding including minor status, temporary absences, ties, but erred on law practice citizenship need.

propositions.text: Evidence here could reasonably establish strong family nexus and state of dependency, unlike in Naveen
Ms Naveen was 23 when she became permanent resident, left home at 19 to study, then attended Harvard Medical School
Ms Naveen never worked in Canada but worked in US as residence advisor, teaching assistant, research mentor
No evidence showed Respondent was dependent on her parents to subsidize her education

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence here supports dependency unlike in Naveen, where Ms Naveen was independent and no evidence showed dependency on parents.

propositions.text: Respondent was a minor on arrival and presumably more dependent on parents than a young adult who left home earlier
No documentary evidence before Citizenship judge showed Respondent was financially dependent on parents
Letter from Respondent's parents and citizenship application confirmed Respondent was supported by parents throughout education
Citizenship judge reasonably accepted Respondent was dependent on parents without further corroboration
Parents offered to provide additional bank statements to prove dependence if required

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Respondent was a minor and dependent; rejects Applicant's claim of no evidence; finds judge reasonably accepted dependency based on parents' letter and application.

propositions.text: Respondent returned home regularly, at least twice annually
This differs from Naveen where Respondent repeatedly failed to return when opportunities arose

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Respondent returned home regularly, unlike Naveen who failed to return repeatedly.

propositions.text: Citizenship judge interviewed Respondent and assessed her commitment to Canada
Judge concluded Respondent centralized living in Canada and was significantly engaged with Canadian society
Whether Citizenship judge could reasonably come to his conclusion on the record before him
Judge's reasons, though could be more articulate, are intelligible and supported by evidence
Reasons are defensible and meet standard of reasonableness

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Citizenship judge reasonably concluded Respondent centralized living in Canada; reasons are defensible and meet reasonableness standard.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is dismissed without costs

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for judicial review without costs.
